title: Effects of functionally distinct dietary fibers in starch-containing meals on medium-chain triglyceride (MCT)-induced ketone body synthesis
summary:
The ketogenic diet is a dietary approach characterised by a high intake of fat, a low intake of carbohydrates and a moderate intake of protein. Ketogenic diets are used to treat various conditions, such as drug-resistant epilepsy. Under this dietary regime, the body produces ketone bodies, which it can use for energy instead of glucose, as is the case with a standard diet. The ketogenic diet mimics a state of fasting in the body. It is known that certain fats (medium-chain triglycerides, MCTs) support the production of ketone bodies. This study investigates the effect of MCTs, when consumed alongside the carbohydrate starch and various types of dietary fibre (beta-glucan, cellulose, inulin), on the production of ketone bodies. The findings are intended, amongst other things, to help make the highly restrictive nature of the ketogenic diet more manageable through the use of MCTs, by allowing potentially larger amounts of carbohydrates to be consumed through the simultaneous intake of dietary fibre.

Following an overnight fast, participants receive a pudding-based meal on each study day, consisting of water, low-fat milk, cornstarch, one type of dietary fiber (except for the control), and either medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) or high-oleic sunflower oil (control). This is followed by a five-hour fasting period. Different dietary fiber sources are tested at standardized doses in combination with standardized amounts of MCTs and carbohydrates. Each participant completes a total of five study days and receives each intervention once. Various metabolic parameters are measured in venous and capillary blood, breath, subcutaneous interstitial fluid, and urine. An adaptive approach is used to ensure that moderate ketone body concentrations are achieved.

Study participants include young, healthy, normal-weight adults up to the age of 40 with no pre-existing conditions, who follow a diet without any noticeable reduction in carbohydrate intake.

The aim is to investigate the effects of individual dietary fiber sources, administered alongside starch, on MCT-induced ketone body production. The primary objective is to assess the effect of beta-glucan compared with a fiber-free control, both in combination with MCTs. Secondarily, the effects of the other dietary fiber sources on ketone body synthesis and additional metabolic parameters are investigated.
conditions: No disease or health problem is being investigated. Investigation of the effect of starch, MCTs and various types of dietary fibre on the metabolism of healthy participants.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Normal weight (BMI = 18.5 – 25.0)
Exclusion criteria:
- Pregnancy, breastfeeding
- Presence of a serious or chronic condition causing significant health impairments (e.g. cancer, cardiovascular disease, thyroid disorders, bowel diseases) or an acute illness at the time of the examination
- Known metabolic disorder (e.g. lipid metabolism disorder, type 1 or 2 diabetes mellitus)
- Taking medication (exception: contraceptives)
- Consumption of MCT within the past 4 weeks
- Mental or speech impairments
- Low-carb or other dietary regimens involving a sustained reduction in carbohydrate intake (EFSA: at least 45% of energy from carbohydrates)
- Diagnosed eating disorders
- Known swallowing disorders or conditions involving clinically significant dysphagia or an increased risk of aspiration
- Donation of whole blood within the last 3 months and/or donation of blood plasma within the last 4 weeks prior to the start of the study
- Intolerance to sucralose or other sweeteners
- Difficult or impossible venous blood sampling due to anatomical conditions or other medical reasons (e.g. veins that are difficult to locate, fragile or severely sclerosed)
- Severe fear of blood sampling or injections
- Functional bowel disorders (particularly irritable bowel syndrome), lactose intolerance, milk protein allergy
